final_proof:
The assertion about equations is valid in the usual setting of linear differential operators over a differential field, but the proposed proof is not: adding equations does not give an equivalent system. The assertion about inequations is false if the resulting inequation is required to remain linear.

Let \((K,\partial)\) be a differential field, and let
\[
R=K[\partial]
\]
be the ring of linear differential operators, with multiplication given by composition and the rule \(\partial a=a\partial+\partial(a)\). The operators may act on any differential field extension of \(K\). We first prove the correct statement for equations.

**Binary reduction lemma.** Given \(P,Q\in R\) and \(x\)-free elements \(f,g\), there are an operator \(D\), an \(x\)-free element \(h\), and an \(x\)-free conjunction \(\chi\) such that
\[
(Px=f\ \land\ Qx=g)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad(Dx=h\ \land\ \chi).
\]

Suppose first that \(P\) and \(Q\) are not both zero. The left ideal
\[
RP+RQ=\{AP+BQ:A,B\in R\}
\]
is principal. Indeed, choose in it a nonzero operator \(D\) of least order. Left division by \(D\) is possible: if \(T\in R\), repeatedly subtract a suitable left multiple of \(D\) to cancel the leading term, obtaining
\[
T=SD+T_0,\qquad \operatorname{ord}(T_0)<\operatorname{ord}(D).
\]
If \(T\in RP+RQ\), then \(T_0=T-SD\) also belongs to that ideal, so the minimality of \(D\) forces \(T_0=0\). Thus \(RP+RQ=RD\). Consequently there are \(A,B,P_1,Q_1\in R\) such that
\[
D=AP+BQ,\qquad P=P_1D,\qquad Q=Q_1D.
\]
Thus \(D\) is a greatest common right divisor of \(P,Q\), with no particular normalization required. Put
\[
h=A(f)+B(g)
\]
and let
\[
\chi:\quad P_1(h)=f\ \land\ Q_1(h)=g.
\]
This condition contains no \(x\). If \(Px=f\) and \(Qx=g\), then
\[
Dx=A(Px)+B(Qx)=A(f)+B(g)=h,
\]
and hence
\[
P_1(h)=P_1(Dx)=Px=f,\qquad Q_1(h)=Q_1(Dx)=Qx=g.
\]
Conversely, if \(Dx=h\) and \(\chi\) holds, then
\[
Px=P_1(Dx)=P_1(h)=f,\qquad Qx=Q_1(Dx)=Q_1(h)=g.
\]
This proves the equivalence. If \(P=Q=0\), take \(D=0\), \(h=0\), and \(\chi\) to be \(f=0\land g=0\); the same conclusion is immediate. This proves the lemma in all cases.

We may now use genuine induction. For one equation there is nothing to prove. Suppose the first \(k\) equations have already been written as
\[
Px=f\ \land\ \psi,
\]
where \(\psi\) contains no \(x\). Then the system of \(k+1\) equations is equivalent to
\[
Px=f\ \land\ P_{k+1}x=f_{k+1}\ \land\ \psi.
\]
Apply the independently proved binary lemma to the two displayed equations containing \(x\). It replaces them by one equation \(Dx=h\) and an \(x\)-free conjunction \(\chi\). Hence the whole system is
\[
Dx=h\ \land\ (\chi\land\psi),
\]
which has the required form. This argument does not invoke the induction hypothesis on a two-equation system; the two-equation case was proved separately in the lemma, so there is no circularity.

The addition argument in the question is invalid even for order-zero operators. Over \(\mathbb Q\), the system
\[
x=0\ \land\ x=1
\]
has no solution, whereas its sum \(2x=1\) has the solution \(x=\tfrac12\). Addition therefore gives only a necessary consequence of the conjunction, not an equivalent equation.

For inequations, the proposed linear normal form is false in general. Take \(K=\mathbb Q\) with the zero derivation and consider
\[
x\ne0\ \land\ x\ne1. \tag{1}
\]
Suppose that (1) were equivalent over \(K\) to
\[
Lx\ne g\ \land\ \psi, \tag{2}
\]
where \(\psi\) contains no \(x\) and \(L=\sum_{i=0}^m a_i\partial^i\) is a linear differential operator. The solution set of (1) is nonempty, so \(\psi\) must be true. Since the derivation is zero, for every \(x\in\mathbb Q\),
\[
Lx=a_0x.
\]
If \(a_0\ne0\), the inequation \(Lx\ne g\) excludes exactly the one value \(g/a_0\). If \(a_0=0\), it excludes either every value or no value, according as \(g=0\) or \(g\ne0\). Thus (2) can define only the empty set, all of \(\mathbb Q\), or \(\mathbb Q\) with one point removed. But (1) defines \(\mathbb Q\setminus\{0,1\}\), a contradiction.

There is, however, a simple correct nonlinear replacement. In any differential field,
\[
\bigwedge_{j=1}^n(P_jx\ne g_j)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\prod_{j=1}^n(P_jx-g_j)\ne0,
\]
because a field has no zero divisors. The expression on the right is generally a nonlinear differential polynomial in \(x\), not a linear expression \(Lx-g\).

Finally, introducing nonzero residuals \(a,b\) does not repair the linear argument. Even if one writes \(Px=f+a\) and \(Qx=g+b\) with \(a,b\ne0\), it may happen that \(a+b=0\), so the sum need not be nonzero. Requiring \(a,b>0\) is unavailable in an arbitrary differential field and, even over an ordered field, would not represent inequations whose residuals are negative. Thus the equation statement needs the binary Euclidean reduction above, while the inequation statement is correct only after allowing the generally nonlinear product.
